newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan economic reforms seen causing stagflation.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan economic reforms seen causing stagflation.

text.p: Pakistan's latest economic reform package is likely to cause stagflation, but should improve the trade and fiscal balance in three to six months, James Capel Asia said in a research report received on Tuesday.
"The increase in the State Bank's discount rate and withholding import tax, together with the devaluation of the rupee will probably have stagflationary effects," it said.

The report was analysing the likely impact of last week's economic stabilisation package, which included a 7.86 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar, an increase in the central bank's key repo rate to 20 percent from 17 and measures to cut the budget deficit by 40 billion rupees ($995 million).
The budget-cutting steps included spending cuts, new taxes and a 10 percent increase in fuel prices.

"The increase in prices of fuel and energy will immediately translate into higher inflation, raise the cost of essential consumer items and industrial inputs and will probably curb imports of non-essential items," the report said.

James Capel said the government's announcement that it would collect at least two billion rupees in agricultural income tax from the four provinces was a positive breakthrough, but its sincerity and effectiveness was doubtful.
"There is no machinery in place to collect this tax and the relevant provincial governments have yet to pass the necessary legislation," the report said.
Three provinces have passed laws since 1994 to collect tax on agriculture income but Punjab, Pakistan's most populous and fertile province, has strongly resisted such attempts.

The James Capel report said that actual inflation was running at 19 percent, even though official figures show the consumer price index falling to 9.83 percent year-on-year in September against 12.49 percent a year earlier.
It said the reforms inspired by the International Monetary Fund might re-establish fiscal discipline by cutting the deficit and reducing government reliance on domestic bank borrowing.
An IMF mission arrived in Islamabad on Saturday to review the economy, a necessary prelude to any renewed disbursements of a stalled $600 million standby loan.
The IMF is known to have shown scepticism at some of the government's economic data and James Capel said a change in Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's economic team was imminent.
On Monday Bhutto gave up the finance portfolio she had held for three years and named Privatisation Minister Syed Naveed Qamar, 41, as Minister for Finance and Economic Affairs.
